Copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate, CuSO4 • 5 H2O, is a blue crystalline solid. Upon gentle heating, it loses water to form anhydrous CuSO4, which is a white solid.
a. When 5.000 g CuSO4 • 5H2O is heated to remove all of its water, what mass of anhydrous CuSO4 will be produced?
b. Explain the change in color on dehydration of CuSO4 • 5 H2O.
c. A solution of 0.0506 g Cu(CH3COO)2 • H2O is made up with water to a volume of 5.00 mL water. This solution in a 1-cm cuvette produces a visible spectrum with a maximum absorption at 763 nm. What wavelength would be the best choice to determine the concentration of Cu(II)?
d. A student determines the value of n in an unknown crystalline hydrate of copper(II) nitrate, Cu(NO3)2 • n H2O, by preparing 5.00 mL of an aqueous solution of a known mass of the compound and measuring its absorbance at the wavelength determined in part c. However, the student inserts the cuvette into the spectrophotometer without first wiping fingerprints from it. How will this affect the value of n determined in the experiment?
e. An alternative method for determining the degree of hydration of the copper nitrate is to allow a known mass of compound to react with excess KI solution, which produces a yellow-brown suspension. Write a balanced net ionic equation for this reaction.
f. The experiment in part e is carried out with 0.1000 g of the hydrated copper(II) nitrate. To the resulting mixture is added a 0.0250 M solution of sodium thiosulfate, Na2S2O3, until the color of the mixture has just dissipated, leaving a milky white suspension. This requires 17.20 mL of added sodium thiosulfate solution. What is the value of n for the Cu(NO3)2 • n H2O?

a. 3.196 g
b. Dehydration changes the ligand environment around Cu(II) from water to sulfate; the d-d absorption shifts out of the visible/into the near-IR, so the solid appears white.
c. 763 nm
d. It will give a smaller value of n.
e. 2 Cu2+(aq) + 5 I-(aq) -> 2 CuI(s) + I3-(aq)
f. n = 2.50

# USNCO 2025 Part 2, Question 1

## Part a: Mass of Anhydrous CuSO₄

**Molar masses:**
- CuSO₄·5H₂O = 63.55 + 32.07 + 4(16.00) + 5(18.015) = **249.69 g/mol**
- CuSO₄ = 63.55 + 32.07 + 4(16.00) = **159.62 g/mol**

$$\text{Mass CuSO}_4 = 5.000 \text{ g} \times \frac{159.62}{249.69} = \boxed{3.196 \text{ g}}$$

---

## Part b: Color Change Explanation

In CuSO₄·5H₂O, the Cu²⁺ ion is coordinated by water molecules (forming [Cu(H₂O)₄]²⁺ or [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ chromophores). The crystal field splitting caused by water ligands produces d–d transitions that absorb red/orange light (~600–800 nm), making the compound appear **blue**. Upon dehydration, the Cu²⁺ coordination environment changes to sulfate oxygen donors, which produce a different (weaker/more uniform) absorption across the visible spectrum, causing the solid to appear **white**.

---

## Part c: Best Wavelength

To determine concentration using Beer–Lambert law ($A = \varepsilon bc$), the **wavelength of maximum absorbance** provides the greatest sensitivity and most reliable adherence to the law.

$$\boxed{\lambda = 763 \text{ nm}}$$

---

## Part d: Effect of Fingerprints

Fingerprints scatter and absorb light, causing the measured absorbance to be **artificially high**. This leads to an **overestimate** of [Cu²⁺] via Beer–Lambert law, hence an overestimate of moles of Cu²⁺ (and moles of compound). Since molar mass = mass/moles, the calculated molar mass is **too low**, and therefore the determined value of **n will be too low**.

---

## Part e: Balanced Net Ionic Equation

Cu²⁺ is reduced to Cu⁺ (precipitated as CuI), and I⁻ is oxidized to I₂:

$$\boxed{2\,\text{Cu}^{2+}(aq) + 4\,\text{I}^-(aq) \longrightarrow 2\,\text{CuI}(s) + \text{I}_2(aq)}$$

(CuI is insoluble and appears as a yellow-brown precipitate, consistent with the observed suspension.)

---

## Part f: Determination of n

**Step 1 — Titration stoichiometry:**

The I₂ produced reacts with thiosulfate:
$$\text{I}_2 + 2\,\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-} \longrightarrow 2\,\text{I}^- + \text{S}_4\text{O}_6^{2-}$$

From the net ionic equation in (e): 2 mol Cu²⁺ → 1 mol I₂ → 2 mol S₂O₃²⁻

$$\therefore \quad n_{\text{Cu}^{2+}} = n_{\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}}$$

**Step 2 — Moles of thiosulfate:**

$$n_{\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}} = 0.0250 \text{ M} \times 0.01720 \text{ L} = 4.300 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$

**Step 3 — Molar mass of the hydrate:**

$$M = \frac{0.1000 \text{ g}}{4.300 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}} = 232.56 \text{ g/mol}$$

**Step 4 — Solve for n:**

$$M_{\text{Cu(NO}_3)_2} = 63.55 + 2(14.01) + 6(16.00) = 187.57 \text{ g/mol}$$

$$n = \frac{232.56 - 187.57}{18.015} = \frac{45.00}{18.015} \approx 2.50$$

$$\boxed{n = 2.5}$$

The unknown hydrate is **Cu(NO₃)₂ · 2.5 H₂O** (i.e., Cu₂(NO₃)₄ · 5H₂O when written with integer subscripts).

# USNCO 2025 Part 2, Question 2

## Part a: Lewis Structure of C₂O₄²⁻

**Total valence electrons:** 2(4) + 4(6) + 2 = **38 electrons**

```
    ⁻O    O
      \\ //
       C — C
      // \\
    O     O⁻
```

Each carbon is bonded to the other C, one C=O double bond, and one C–O⁻ single bond (with resonance). In one resonance form:

- **Each =O:** 2 lone pairs, formal charge **0**
- **Each –O⁻:** 3 lone pairs, formal charge **−1**
- **Each C:** 0 lone pairs, formal charge **0**
- Two equivalent resonance structures exist (double bonds can swap positions on each carboxylate)

Check: 2(0) + 2(0) + 2(−1) = **−2** ✓

---

## Part b: Molar Solubility in Pure Water

$$\text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Ca}^{2+}(aq) + \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}(aq)$$

$$K_{sp} = s^2 \implies s = \sqrt{2.7 \times 10^{-9}}$$

$$\boxed{s = 5.2 \times 10^{-5} \text{ M}}$$

---

## Part c: Molar Solubility in 0.100 M CaCl₂

Common-ion effect with [Ca²⁺] = 0.100 M (from CaCl₂):

$$K_{sp} = (0.100)(s) \implies s = \frac{2.7 \times 10^{-9}}{0.100}$$

$$\boxed{s = 2.7 \times 10^{-8} \text{ M}}$$

---

## Part d: pH of the Final Solution

When all 0.100 mol CaC₂O₄ just dissolves in 1.00 L, the solution is **exactly at saturation**:

$$[\text{Ca}^{2+}] = 0.100 \text{ M}, \qquad [\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}] = \frac{K_{sp}}{[\text{Ca}^{2+}]} = \frac{2.7 \times 10^{-9}}{0.100} = 2.7 \times 10^{-8} \text{ M}$$

Since $[\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}]$ is extremely small, virtually all oxalate is protonated to H₂C₂O₄, so $[\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4] \approx 0.100$ M. Using the overall equilibrium:

$$K_{a1} \cdot K_{a2} = \frac{[\text{H}^+]^2[\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}]}{[\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4]}$$

$$[\text{H}^+]^2 = \frac{K_{a1} \cdot K_{a2} \cdot [\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4]}{[\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}]} = \frac{(5.37 \times 10^{-2})(5.25 \times 10^{-5})(0.100)}{2.7 \times 10^{-8}} = 10.44$$

$$[\text{H}^+] = 3.23 \text{ M} \implies \boxed{pH = -0.51}$$

---

## Part e: Moles of HCl Added

From **charge balance** (all Cl⁻ comes from HCl):

$$[\text{Cl}^-] = 2[\text{Ca}^{2+}] + [\text{H}^+] - [\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-] - 2[\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}] - [\text{OH}^-]$$

First, $[\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-] = \dfrac{[\text{H}^+][\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}]}{K_{a2}} = \dfrac{(3.23)(2.7 \times 10^{-8})}{5.25 \times 10^{-5}} = 1.66 \times 10^{-3}$ M

$$[\text{Cl}^-] = 0.200 + 3.23 - 0.0017 - 0 - 0 = 3.43 \text{ M}$$

$$\boxed{n_{\text{HCl}} \approx 3.43 \text{ mol}}$$

---

## Part f: Solubility in 0.1 M NaHC₂O₄

**The solubility will be significantly less than in pure water.**

**Justification:** In 0.1 M NaHC₂O₄, the amphoteric HC₂O₄⁻ partially dissociates (via $K_{a2} = 5.25 \times 10^{-5}$) to produce C₂O₄²⁻. At the approximate solution pH of $(\text{p}K_{a1} + \text{p}K_{a2})/2 = 2.78$:

$$[\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}] \approx \alpha_2 \times 0.1 \approx 0.030 \times 0.1 \approx 3 \times 10^{-3} \text{ M}$$

This **common-ion** C₂O₄²⁻ concentration (~3 × 10⁻³ M) is roughly **60 times larger** than the [C₂O₄²⁻] at saturation in pure water (5.2 × 10⁻⁵ M). The elevated [C₂O₄²⁻] drives $[\text{Ca}^{2+}][\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}]$ to exceed $K_{sp}$ at much lower Ca²⁺ concentrations, suppressing dissolution via the common-ion effect:

$$s_{\max} = \frac{K_{sp}}{[\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}]} \approx \frac{2.7 \times 10^{-9}}{3 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 10^{-6} \text{ M} \ll 5.2 \times 10^{-5} \text{ M}$$

# USNCO 2025 Part 2, Question 3

## Part a: ΔG°rxn at 298 K

**Reaction:** DMEA(aq) + CH₃COOH(aq) → DMEAH⁺(aq) + CH₃COO⁻(aq)

**Equilibrium constant** — break into two steps where H⁺ cancels:

$$K = \frac{K_a(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH})}{K_a(\text{DMEAH}^+)} = \frac{1.8 \times 10^{-5}}{6.0 \times 10^{-10}} = 3.0 \times 10^{4}$$

$$\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K = -(8.314)(298)\ln(3.0\times10^4) = -(2477.6)(10.31)$$

$$\boxed{\Delta G^\circ_{rxn} = -25.5 \text{ kJ/mol}}$$

---

## Part b: ΔH°rxn

**Identifying the equivalence point:**
- $n(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}) = 7.84/60.05 = 0.1306$ mol
- $n(\text{DMEA at 12 g}) = 12/89.14 = 0.1346$ mol

These are approximately equal, confirming CH₃COOH is the limiting reagent.

**Temperature change:**
- $T_i = 19.03\,°\text{C}$ (from linear fit at $x = 0$)
- $T_f = 31.84\,°\text{C}$ (plateau)
- $\Delta T = 12.81\,°\text{C}$

**Total mass of solution at equivalence:**

$$m = 7.84 + 107.17 + 12.00 = 127.01 \text{ g}$$

**Heat absorbed by solution (well-insulated → $q_{rxn} = -q_{solution}$):**

$$q = mc\Delta T = (127.01)(4.184)(12.81) = 6807 \text{ J}$$

$$\Delta H^\circ_{rxn} = \frac{-6807 \text{ J}}{0.1306 \text{ mol}}$$

$$\boxed{\Delta H^\circ_{rxn} \approx -52.1 \text{ kJ/mol}}$$

---

## Part c: ΔS°rxn

Using $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$:

$$\Delta S^\circ = \frac{\Delta H^\circ - \Delta G^\circ}{T} = \frac{-52.1 - (-25.5)}{298} = \frac{-26.6 \text{ kJ/mol}}{298 \text{ K}}$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S^\circ_{rxn} \approx -89.3 \text{ J/(mol·K)}}$$

---

## Part d: Why ΔS° is Negative

The reaction converts **two neutral molecules** into **two ions**:

$$\underbrace{\text{DMEA} + \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}}_{\text{neutral molecules}} \longrightarrow \underbrace{\text{DMEAH}^+ + \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-}_{\text{ions}}$$

Although the number of solute particles is conserved (2 → 2), the critical feature is the **creation of charge**. Product ions exert strong **ion–dipole forces** on surrounding water molecules, causing **electrostriction** — water molecules become tightly organized into ordered hydration shells around each ion. The reactant neutral molecules, interacting with water only through weaker hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces, cause far less solvent ordering. This **net increase in solvent structure** dominates, producing the observed negative $\Delta S°$.

judge_result.evidence: The candidate correctly solved Part a and provided an excellent explanation of solvation and electrostriction in Part d. Correct formulas were utilized throughout the response.
judge_result.deductions: In Part b, the candidate used 12.00 g instead of calculating the intersection mass (11.23 g), causing propagated errors in heat, enthalpy, and entropy calculations.

# USNCO 2025 Part 2, Question 4

## Part a: Anode and Cathode

From the given cell reaction Zn(s) + Pb²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Pb(s):

$$\boxed{\text{Anode: Zn electrode} \quad | \quad \text{Cathode: Pb electrode}}$$

Zn is **oxidized** (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻) at the anode; Pb²⁺ is **reduced** (Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb) at the cathode.

---

## Part b: Standard Reduction Potential for Pb²⁺

At 298 K (standard conditions with 1.00 M solutions):

$$E^\circ_{cell} = 0.7887 - 0.000515(298) = 0.7887 - 0.1535 = 0.635 \text{ V}$$

$$E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ(\text{Pb}^{2+}/\text{Pb}) - E^\circ(\text{Zn}^{2+}/\text{Zn})$$

$$0.635 = E^\circ(\text{Pb}^{2+}/\text{Pb}) - (-0.762)$$

$$\boxed{E^\circ(\text{Pb}^{2+}/\text{Pb}) = -0.127 \text{ V}}$$

---

## Part c: ∆G°, ∆H°, and ∆S°

For the reaction with **n = 2** electrons transferred:

$$\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{cell} = -(2)(96{,}485)(0.635)$$

$$\boxed{\Delta G^\circ = -122.5 \text{ kJ/mol}}$$

For ∆H° and ∆S°, use the temperature-dependent Gibbs relation. Since $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE = -nF(0.7887 - 0.000515\,T)$:

$$\Delta G^\circ = \underbrace{-nF(0.7887)}_{\Delta H^\circ} + \underbrace{nF(0.000515)}_{-\Delta S^\circ}\cdot T$$

Matching term-by-term with $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$:

$$\Delta H^\circ = -nF(0.7887) = -(2)(96{,}485)(0.7887)$$

$$\boxed{\Delta H^\circ = -152.2 \text{ kJ/mol}}$$

$$\Delta S^\circ = -nF(0.000515) = -(2)(96{,}485)(0.000515)$$

$$\boxed{\Delta S^\circ = -99.4 \text{ J/(mol·K)}}$$

*Verification:* $\Delta G^\circ = -152.2 - (298)(-0.0994) = -152.2 + 29.6 = -122.6$ kJ/mol ✓

---

## Part d: Why ∆S° is Negative

The reaction converts Zn(s) + Pb²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Pb(s): one ion in solution replaces another, and one solid replaces another, so the **number** of each type of species is unchanged.

The critical difference is **ionic size**: Zn²⁺ (radius ≈ 74 pm) is much **smaller** than Pb²⁺ (radius ≈ 119 pm), giving Zn²⁺ a significantly **higher charge density** despite both having a +2 charge. The higher charge density of Zn²⁺ produces **stronger ion–dipole interactions** with surrounding water, creating a **more extensively ordered hydration shell** compared to Pb²⁺. This increase in solvent structure upon replacing Pb²⁺(aq) with Zn²⁺(aq) is the dominant factor causing ∆S° < 0. (Standard ionic entropies confirm this: S°(Zn²⁺, aq) ≈ −112 J/(mol·K) vs. S°(Pb²⁺, aq) ≈ +10 J/(mol·K).)

---

## Part e: Non-Standard Cell (0.100 M Pb²⁺)

With [Zn²⁺] = 1.00 M and [Pb²⁺] = 0.100 M, the Nernst equation gives:

$$E = E^\circ(T) - \frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q = (0.7887 - 0.000515\,T) - \frac{RT}{2F}\ln(10)$$

Since $\frac{R\ln 10}{2F} = \frac{8.314 \times 2.303}{192{,}970} = 9.92 \times 10^{-5}$ V/K is a constant, the new expression is:

$$E = 0.7887 - 0.000614\,T$$

**The new plot is:**
- Still **linear** in $T$
- Has the **same y-intercept** (0.7887 V) as the standard cell
- Has a **more negative (steeper) slope**: −0.000614 V/K vs. −0.000515 V/K

**Justification:** The Nernst correction $-\frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q$ with $Q = 10 > 1$ is negative and **proportional to $T$**. It lowers $E$ at every temperature, and the lowering grows with increasing $T$, steepening the slope while leaving the $T = 0$ intercept unchanged.

Write net equations for each of the reactions below. Use appropriate ionic and molecular formulas and omit formulas for all ions or molecules that do not take part in a reaction. Write structural formulas for all organic substances, and clearly show stereochemistry where relevant. You need not balance the equations or show the phases of the species.
a. Carbon dioxide is bubbled through a saturated solution of barium hydroxide.
b. Potassium permanganate is mixed with iron(II) sulfate in dilute sulfuric acid.

# USNCO 2025 Part 2, Question 6

## Part a: Why O₂ has a higher boiling point than N₂ or F₂

All three are nonpolar diatomic molecules, so the only intermolecular forces are **London dispersion forces**, which increase with **polarizability**.

O₂ has **two unpaired electrons** in its degenerate π\* antibonding orbitals. These unpaired electrons occupy relatively diffuse orbitals that are **easily distorted**, making O₂ significantly more polarizable than expected for its size. Although F₂ has more electrons (18 vs. 16), its electrons are all **paired** in more tightly held orbitals, resulting in lower polarizability. N₂ (14 electrons, all paired) is the least polarizable of the three.

Thus the enhanced polarizability from O₂'s unpaired electrons gives it the strongest London dispersion forces, explaining the anomalous boiling point order: **N₂ (77 K) < F₂ (85 K) < O₂ (90 K)**.

---

## Part b: Two unpaired electrons in both O and O₂

**Atomic oxygen:** Electron configuration 1s²2s²2p⁴. By **Hund's rule**, the four 2p electrons distribute across three degenerate orbitals as ↑↓, ↑, ↑ — giving **two unpaired electrons**.

**Molecular oxygen:** In MO theory, O₂ has configuration $(\sigma_{2p})^2(\pi_{2p})^4(\pi^*_{2p})^2$. The last two electrons occupy the two **degenerate π\* orbitals**. By **Hund's rule**, they occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins: π\*_x(↑), π\*_y(↑) — giving **two unpaired electrons**.

In both cases, Hund's rule applied to a set of **degenerate orbitals** with a specific electron count forces two electrons to remain unpaired.

---

## Part c: Energy of the ¹Δg excited state

The excited state (singlet O₂, no unpaired electrons) emits at λ = 1270 nm:

$$E = \frac{N_A hc}{\lambda} = \frac{(6.022\times10^{23})(6.626\times10^{-34})(2.998\times10^{8})}{1270\times10^{-9}}$$

$$= \frac{0.1196 \text{ J·mol}^{-1}\text{·m}}{1.270\times10^{-6}\text{ m}} = 94{,}173 \text{ J/mol}$$

$$\boxed{E \approx 94.2 \text{ kJ/mol}}$$

---

## Part d: Why O₂ is IR-inactive but O₃ is IR-active

A molecule absorbs infrared radiation only if a vibration produces a **change in dipole moment** (∂μ/∂q ≠ 0).

**O₂** is a homonuclear diatomic molecule — it has no dipole moment, and its only vibrational mode (bond stretching) preserves the symmetry, producing **no change in dipole moment**. Therefore O₂ is **IR-inactive**.

**O₃** is a bent, asymmetric triatomic molecule with a permanent dipole moment. Its asymmetric stretch and bending modes produce **changes in dipole moment**, making them **IR-active**. (In contrast, N₂ and CO₂'s symmetric stretches are IR-inactive, but CO₂'s asymmetric stretch is IR-active — analogous to the O₃ case.)

---

## Part e: Bond distance assignments

Using the relationship between **bond order and bond distance**:

| Species | Bond Order | Distance | Justification |
|---------|-----------|----------|---------------|
| **O₂⁺** | 2.5 | **112 pm** | Highest BO (removed antibonding π\* electron); shortest bond |
| **O₂** | 2.0 | **121 pm** | Double bond (2 bonds in MO theory) |
| **O₂⁻** | 1.5 | **127 pm** | One electron added to π\*; BO = (10−7)/2 = 1.5 |
| **O₃** | ≈1.5 | **128 pm** | Resonance hybrid: O=O–O⁻ ↔ ⁻O–O=O gives effective BO ≈ 1.5 |
| **O₃⁻** | <1.5 | **135 pm** | Extra electron enters antibonding MO, lowering BO below that of O₃ |
| **O₂²⁻** | 1.0 | **154 pm** | Peroxide: BO = (10−8)/2 = 1; longest bond |

**Key justifications:**

1. **Dioxygen series** (O₂⁺ → O₂ → O₂⁻ → O₂²⁻): Each successive reduction adds an electron to a **π\* antibonding orbital**, decreasing bond order by 0.5 each step and **systematically increasing** bond distance (112 → 121 → 127 → 154 pm).

2. **O₂⁻ ≈ O₃**: Both have effective bond order ~1.5, so their distances are essentially identical (127 ≈ 128 pm), consistent with the problem's allowance to treat these as the same.

3. **O₃⁻ > O₃**: The extra electron in O₃⁻ occupies an **antibonding orbital**, reducing the effective bond order below 1.5 and lengthening the bond (135 pm vs. 128 pm).

4. **O₂²⁻ is longest**: With bond order = 1 (a true single bond), it has the weakest bonding and the **longest distance** (154 pm).

# USNCO 2025 Part 2, Question 7

## Part a: Sphere Identification in CsPbI₃

In a perovskite unit cell (ABX₃):

| Position | Count | Sphere type | Element |
|----------|-------|-------------|---------|
| 8 corners | 8 × ⅛ = **1** | Small gray | **Cs⁺** (A-site cation) |
| 6 face centers | 6 × ½ = **3** | Medium white | **I⁻** (X-site anion) |
| 1 body center | 1 × 1 = **1** | Large black | **Pb²⁺** (B-site cation) |

---

## Part b: Coordination Numbers

**Pb²⁺ (body center):**
- Coordination number: **6**
- Nearest neighbors: **6 I⁻** ions at the face centers (octahedral arrangement, Pb–I distance = a/2 = 314 pm)

**I⁻ (face centers):**
- Coordination number: **2** (for Pb²⁺)
- Nearest neighbors: **2 Pb²⁺** ions at the body centers of adjacent unit cells (I is shared between two octahedra)
- Also has **8 Cs⁺** neighbors at slightly greater distance (at corners)

**Cs⁺ (corners):**
- Coordination number: **12**
- Nearest neighbors: **12 I⁻** ions at the face centers of adjacent unit cells (cuboctahedral arrangement)

---

## Part c: Density

$$d = \frac{ZM}{N_A \cdot a^3}$$

- Z = 1 formula unit per unit cell
- M(CsPbI₃) = 132.91 + 207.2 + 3(126.90) = 620.81 g/mol
- a = 628 pm = 6.28 × 10⁻⁸ cm

$$d = \frac{(1)(620.81)}{(6.022\times10^{23})(6.28\times10^{-8})^3} = \frac{620.81}{(6.022\times10^{23})(2.477\times10^{-22})}$$

$$\boxed{d = 4.15 \text{ g/cm}^3}$$

---

## Part d: Sphere Identification in YBa₂Cu₃O₇

| Sphere type | Count | Element | Justification |
|-------------|-------|---------|---------------|
| **A** (central layer, ×1) | 1 | **Y** | Largest rare earth cation, sits at cell center |
| **B** (layers above/below, ×2) | 2 | **Ba** | Second largest cation, sits in layers flanking Y |
| **C** (black, three sites) | 3 | **Cu** | Three crystallographically distinct Cu positions (middle + top/bottom) |
| **D** (small, ×7) | 7 | **O** | Most numerous atoms; sizes consistent with oxide ions |

Verification: YBa₂Cu₃O₇ → 1 + 2 + 3 + 7 = 13 atoms per unit cell ✓

---

## Part e: Oxidation Numbers

**Charge balance:** (+3) + 2(+2) + 3(c) + 7(−2) = 0

$$3 + 4 + 3c - 14 = 0 \implies 3c = +7$$

$$\boxed{c = +\tfrac{7}{3}}$$

| Element | Oxidation Number |
|---------|-----------------|
| Y | **+3** |
| Ba | **+2** |
| Cu | **+7/3** (average) |
| O | **−2** |

---

## Part f: Coordination Geometries and Oxidation States

**The two geometries are:**

1. **Square planar** (4-coordinate) — the top/bottom face Cu atoms have four nearly coplanar O neighbors

2. **Square pyramidal** (5-coordinate) — the middle-layer Cu atoms have four coplanar O neighbors plus one axial O along the vertical direction

**Connection to oxidation numbers:**

The non-integer average Cu oxidation state of **+7/3** indicates copper exists as a **mixture of Cu²⁺ and Cu³⁺** in the structure. The two distinct coordination environments accommodate these two different oxidation states:

- **Cu²⁺ (d⁹)** strongly favors **square planar** geometry due to Jahn–Teller distortion of the octahedral d⁹ configuration (selective elongation along one axis removes the axial ligands entirely)
- **Cu³⁺ (d⁸)** can readily adopt **square pyramidal** (5-coordinate) geometry, as d⁸ systems have no Jahn–Teller driving force and tolerate higher coordination numbers

Thus the observation of **two different coordination geometries is direct structural evidence for mixed copper valence** (+2 and +3), which is the fundamental feature enabling the high-temperature superconducting properties of YBa₂Cu₃O₇.

# USNCO 2025 Part 2, Question 8

## Part a: Monobromination of 3-Methylpentane

**Conditions:** Br₂, UV light (hν) — free-radical bromination

3-Methylpentane has one **tertiary carbon** (C3) and Br₂ is highly selective for 3° C–H bonds. The sole monobromide is **3-bromo-3-methylpentane**:

```
        CH₃
        |
CH₃—CH₂—C—CH₂—CH₃
        |
        Br
```

---

## Part b: Cyclohexene + Br₂ in Different Solvents

**In CCl₄** — standard anti-addition:

**trans-1,2-Dibromocyclohexane** (the two Br atoms are *trans* on the ring):

```
      Br    H
       \   /
        C—C
       /   \
   ...ring...
   (anti/trans addition)
```

**In H₂O** — bromohydrin formation (H₂O acts as nucleophile):

**trans-2-Bromocyclohexanol** (Br and OH are *trans*):

```
      Br    OH
       \   /
        C—C
       /   \
   ...ring...
   (anti addition)
```

In both cases, a **bromonium ion** intermediate forms first, and the nucleophile (Br⁻ or H₂O) attacks from the opposite face, giving **anti (trans)** stereochemistry.

---

## Part c: Benzene + Br₂ + Lewis Acid

**Catalyst:** FeBr₃ (or AlCl₃, FeCl₃, etc.)

**Product:** **Bromobenzene** (electrophilic aromatic substitution):

$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{Br}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{FeBr}_3} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br} + \text{HBr}$$

```
       Br
       |
   ⌀———   (bromobenzene, with HBr as byproduct)
```

---

## Part d: Cyclopentanone + Excess Br₂/Base

**Product: 2,2,5,5-tetrabromocyclopentanone**

Cyclopentanone has **4 α-hydrogens** (2 on each α-carbon). With excess Br₂ and base, all four are replaced:

```
        O
        ‖
        C
       / \
   Br₂C   CBr₂
      |    |
      CH₂—CH₂
```

**Why poor yield of monobromide with 1 equiv Br₂:**

Once one α-hydrogen is replaced by Br, the **electron-withdrawing Br** increases the acidity of the remaining C–H bonds on the **same α-carbon**. In the presence of base, the monobrominated product forms its enolate **faster** than the starting material does. Consequently, the monobrominated intermediate undergoes a second bromination before all the starting ketone has reacted. This cascading effect progressively **pushes the reaction toward the fully brominated product** (2,2,5,5-tetrabromide), making isolation of the monobromide impractical.

---

## Part e: Acetophenone + Excess I₂ + NaOH (Iodoform Reaction)

This is the classic **iodoform reaction**. The methyl ketone CH₃CO– is cleaved by I₂/OH⁻:

$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3 + 3\text{I}_2 + 4\text{NaOH} \longrightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+ + \text{CHI}_3\!\downarrow + 3\text{NaI} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Yellow precipitate — Iodoform (CHI₃):**

```
        I
        |
    I — C — H
        |
        I
```

**Water-soluble organic species — Sodium benzoate (C₆H₅COO⁻Na⁺):**

```
        O⁻ Na⁺
        |
    ⌀ — C
        ‖
        O
```
